For $t < \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, $1 + 2t \le 2\lfloor n/2\rfloor - 1 < w$, so no reduction happens and the value is odd. For larger $t$, $1 + 2t$ lies between $w$ and $2w$, so $A(t) = 1 + 2t - w$, and since $w$ is odd this is even.
:::

**14. [M] Trace the stable partition by rotations on $[5, 2, 8, 3]$ with "even first". What does each level do?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Left half $[5, 2]$: halves $[5]$ (boundary $0$) and $[2]$ (boundary $2$); rotate cells $[0, 2)$ by $1$: $[2, 5]$, boundary $1$. Right half $[8, 3]$: already $[8 \mid 3]$, boundary $3$. Top level: $[2 \mid 5 \mid 8 \mid 3]$ with $F_1 = [5]$ and $T_2 = [8]$; rotate cells $[1, 3)$ by $1$: $[2, 8, 5, 3]$, boundary $2$. Evens $2, 8$ and odds $5, 3$ keep their input order.
:::

**15. [H] Prove that calling next permutation $n!$ times, starting from the sorted array of $n$ distinct values, does $O(n!)$ total work, that is $O(1)$ per call on average.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A call's work is proportional to the length $\ell$ of the longest non-increasing suffix plus one (the two scans and the reversal stay inside it). The suffix of length $\ell$ is decreasing in exactly those permutations whose last $\ell$ values are in decreasing order: a $1/\ell!$ fraction of all permutations. So the number of calls with suffix length at least $\ell$ is at most $n!/\ell!$, and the total work is $O\left(\sum_{\ell \ge 0} n!/\ell!\right) = O(e \cdot n!)$. Hence the average is a constant, and listing all permutations costs $O(n \cdot n!)$ only because each must be printed.
:::

**16. [H] Prove that the block-swap rotation does exactly $n - \gcd(n, k)$ swaps for $0 < k < n$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each round with lengths $(L, k)$, $m = L - k$, swaps $\min(k, m)$ pairs and continues with $(L - k, k)$ if $k < m$, or with $(k, k - m)$ if $k \ge m$. In both cases the pair of block lengths $(k, m)$ becomes $(k, m - k)$ or $(k - m, m)$: the subtraction form of Euclid's algorithm on $(k, m)$, which keeps $\gcd(k, m) = \gcd(n, k)$ and stops when one length is $0$. Just before that, $k = m = g$, and the round swaps $g$ pairs and fixes $2g$ elements; every earlier round fixes exactly as many elements as it swaps. All $n$ elements are fixed at the end, so the swaps total $n - g$.
:::

**17. [H] Prove that a permutation of $1..n$ with every adjacent sum composite exists if and only if $n \ge 5$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$n = 2$: the only sum is $3$. $n = 3$: the sums are $3, 4, 5$ for the three pairs; only $\{1, 3\}$ is composite, but a path through three values needs two composite pairs. $n = 4$: the composite pair sums are $1 + 3 = 4$ and $2 + 4 = 6$ only (the others are $3, 5, 5, 7$); two disjoint pairs cannot form a path through four values. $n \ge 5$: evens first, then the odds headed by $o \in \{1, 3, 5\}$ with $E + o \equiv 0 \pmod 3$. Sums inside each block are even and at least $4$, and the seam is a multiple of $3$ that is at least $9$ (@sec-part-p4-b).
:::

**18. [H] After two in-shuffles of $6$ cards, where has the card at index $3$ gone? Answer from the cycle structure, and say after how many shuffles the deck first returns to its starting order.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
One in-shuffle sends $j$ to $(2j + 1) \bmod 7$. Index $3$ is on the cycle $3 \to 0 \to 1 \to 3$, so two shuffles take it to $1$. The other cycle is $2 \to 5 \to 4 \to 2$. Both cycles have length $3$, so after $3$ shuffles every card is home, and not before: the deck's order is the least common multiple of the cycle lengths, $\operatorname{ord}_7(2) = 3$.
:::

## Interview questions

**1. Sort an array of $0$s, $1$s and $2$s in one pass with $O(1)$ extra memory. What is the invariant, and why does the cursor `mid` not move after a swap with `hi`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The Dutch national flag (@sec-part-dnf): regions $[0..\text{lo})$ all $0$, $[\text{lo}..\text{mid})$ all $1$, $[\text{mid}..\text{hi}]$ unknown, $(\text{hi}..n)$ all $2$. Each step shrinks the unknown region by one, so $n$ steps. After `swap(a[mid], a[hi])` the value at `mid` came from the unknown region and has not been classified, so `mid` must look at it again.
:::

**2. Lomuto or Hoare? Name one input where the choice matters.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Hoare does about a third of Lomuto's swaps and splits an all-equal array in the middle, because both fingers stop on keys equal to the pivot; Lomuto sends all equal keys to one side, so quicksort with Lomuto is $\Theta(n^2)$ on all-equal input (@sec-part-a1-compare). Lomuto is simpler and leaves the pivot at its final index, which quickselect likes. With many duplicates, use the three-way partition.
:::

**3. Can you partition stably in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra memory?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Not with the simple walks: Lomuto, Hoare and the Dutch flag all lose the order inside groups. The practical options are an $O(n)$ buffer (append each element to its group) or divide and conquer with rotations, $O(n\log n)$ time in place (@sec-part-stable-rot). Linear-time constant-space stable partitioning exists in the research literature but is far too intricate to write in an interview; naming the trade-off is the expected answer.
:::

**4. Rearrange an array with equal numbers of positives and negatives so that signs alternate, keeping the order inside each sign. What is the simplest $O(n)$ solution?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
One read pass with two write cursors: a positive goes to `res[pw]`, `pw += 2`, starting at $0$; a negative to `res[nw]`, `nw += 2`, starting at $1$ (@sec-part-p2-a). Each class's slots receive its elements in input order, so it is stable. An in-place swap partition would lose that order.
:::

**5. In Sort Array by Parity II, why does one cursor running off the end mean nothing is left to fix?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The array has as many even values as even slots, so the number of even slots holding an odd value equals the number of odd slots holding an even value. Each swap removes one of each, so the two counts stay equal; when one cursor finds no more misplaced cells, the other has none either (@sec-part-p2-b).
:::

**6. Find the next permutation in place. Why is reversing the suffix enough, and what goes wrong with duplicates?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Pivot: rightmost $i$ with $a_i < a_{i+1}$; successor: rightmost $j > i$ with $a_j > a_i$; swap; reverse $a[i+1..n)$ (@sec-part-perm). The suffix is non-increasing before the swap, and the value placed at $j$ is below its left neighbour and at least its right neighbour, so it stays non-increasing and the reversal sorts it. With duplicates both scans must be non-strict; otherwise $[1, 5, 1]$ swaps two equal values and the result is smaller than the input.
:::

**7. Given an integer, find the smallest larger integer with the same digits. What are the traps?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Next permutation on the digit string, $O(d)$ for $d$ digits (@sec-part-p3-b). The traps: no pivot means "no answer" (no wrap-around), and the result can overflow 32 bits (parse into 64 bits, then compare with $2^{31} - 1$). Leading zeros cannot appear, because the result is larger and has as many digits.
:::

**8. How do you get the $k$-th permutation of $1..n$ without stepping $k$ times?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Unrank with factorials (@eq-rank): the first value is the $\lfloor k / (n-1)! \rfloor$-th smallest unused one, then continue with $k \bmod (n-1)!$. $O(n^2)$ with a list, $O(n\log n)$ with a Fenwick tree over the unused values (@sec-part-rank).
:::

**9. Wiggle Sort II: why does "sort and interleave" sometimes fail, and how do you fix it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Interleaving the sorted halves in increasing order puts copies of the middle value side by side in the middle of the array: $[1, 2, 2, 3] \to [1, 2, 2, 3]$. Dealing both halves in decreasing order sends those copies to opposite ends, and they can then meet only if the value occurs more than $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ times, in which case no answer exists (@sec-part-p4-a). For $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space: quickselect the median and run a three-way partition through the virtual index $(1 + 2t) \bmod (n \mid 1)$.
:::

**10. Why is the virtual-index modulus $n \mid 1$ rather than $n$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$t \mapsto 1 + 2t$ must hit every cell once, which needs an odd modulus ($\gcd(2, w) = 1$). For even $n$, the modulus $n$ would visit only odd cells, each twice. $n \mid 1$ is $n + 1$ for even $n$ and $n$ for odd $n$; with $n + 1$, the one extra residue, $n$, is never reached for $t < n$ (@sec-part-virtual).
:::

**11. Compare the three ways to rotate in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space. Which do you write in an interview?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Three reversals: about $2n$ writes, sequential, almost impossible to get wrong; the default. Juggling: exactly $n$ writes, but jumps by $k$ and needs the $\gcd(n, k)$ cycle count. Block swap: $2(n - \gcd(n, k))$ writes in sequential runs, Euclid-shaped (@sec-part-rotate-costs). Write the reversals; mention juggling if the interviewer asks for the fewest writes.
:::

**12. A split by threshold $x$ (all values $< x$ first, both sides keeping their order) is the only operation allowed. How many are needed to sort a permutation?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The number of values $v$ with $\text{pos}[v+1] < \text{pos}[v]$. A split changes the relative order of $v$ and $v+1$ only when $x = v + 1$, so each backwards pair needs its own split, and splitting at each of them once sorts the array (@sec-part-p1-b). $O(n)$ with the inverse permutation.
:::

**13. You may cyclically shift either of two permutations. Why is it enough to try rotations of one of them, and how do you avoid trying all $n$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Shifting $a$ by $s_1$ and $b$ by $s_2$ aligns the same pairs as shifting only $b$ by $s_2 - s_1$, so only the relative offset matters. Each value $v$ matches under exactly one offset, $(\text{pos}_a(v) - \text{pos}_b(v)) \bmod n$; count the votes and take the maximum, $O(n)$ (@sec-part-p5-b).
:::

**14. Make a stable partition with no buffer. What does rotation have to do with it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Divide and conquer: partition both halves stably, giving $T_1 F_1 T_2 F_2$, then rotate the middle $F_1 T_2$ into $T_2 F_1$. Rotations move blocks without changing the order inside them, so the result is stable; the total is $O(n\log n)$ time (@sec-part-stable-rot). This is what `std::stable_partition` does when it cannot allocate memory.
:::

## Summary

::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"}
- **Dutch national flag:** `[< p | = p | unknown | > p]`; less → swap with `lo`, both advance; equal → `mid++`; greater → swap with `hi`, `hi--` only. $O(n)$, $O(1)$, unstable.
- **Stable partition:** read once, append to each group (or one buffer with a write cursor per group). $O(n)$ time, $O(n)$ memory.
- **Slot pattern:** a write cursor per class stepping by $2$ (stable); or two cursors on the two slot classes swapping misplaced pairs (in place).
- **Next permutation:** rightmost $a_i < a_{i+1}$; rightmost $a_j > a_i$; swap; reverse $a[i+1..)$. Previous: mirror the comparisons.
- **Rank:** $\sum c_i (n-1-i)!$ with $c_i$ the unused values below $a_i$; unrank by dividing by factorials.
- **Strict wiggle:** median $m$; three-way `[> m | = m | < m]` over cells $A(t) = (1+2t) \bmod (n \mid 1)$. Or sort and deal both halves reversed.
- **Rotation:** three reversals; juggling over $\gcd(n, k)$ cycles; block swap with $n - \gcd(n, k)$ swaps.
- **Stable in place:** partition the halves, rotate the middle block; $O(n\log n)$.
:::

- Partitioning is *classify, then place*. The classify step is a comparison or a predicate; the place step is blocks, slots, a suffix, or an index map.
- Every partition walk is proved by its invariant: name the regions before writing the cursors.
- Stability is a price, not a free property: the in-place walks lose it; a buffer or rotations buy it back (@sec-part-stable).
- "Any valid arrangement" in a statement is the licence to swap in place; "relative order" is the order to append.
- Next permutation is "change as far right as possible": the non-increasing suffix is the part that cannot change on its own.
- A two-group placement can fail only where the groups touch; find that seam (the median's copies, the even/odd boundary) and the proof is about it alone.
- Rotations move blocks without disturbing their insides, which is why they make stable rearrangement possible without a buffer.
- In-place permutations are cycles: juggling, the perfect shuffle and the virtual index all walk the cycles of an index map, the subject of @sec-idx.

## Further reading

- [Wikipedia — Dutch national flag problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_national_flag_problem) — Dijkstra's problem, the four-region invariant and pseudocode for the three-pointer walk.
- [Wikipedia — Quicksort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quicksort) — Lomuto's and Hoare's partition schemes side by side, with their behaviour on repeated keys.
- [Sedgewick & Wayne, *Algorithms*, §2.3 Quicksort](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/23quicksort/) — three-way partitioning in quicksort and why it makes duplicate-heavy inputs fast.
- [Nayuki — Next lexicographical permutation algorithm](https://www.nayuki.io/page/next-lexicographical-permutation-algorithm) — the four steps with a worked picture and code in several languages.
- [Wikipedia — Lehmer code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehmer_code) — the digits $c_i$ of @eq-rank and the factorial number system behind rank and unrank.
- [cppreference — std::stable_partition](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/algorithm/stable_partition) — the library's stable split and its complexity with and without extra memory.
- [P. Jain, *A Simple In-Place Algorithm for In-Shuffle* (arXiv:0805.1598)](https://arxiv.org/abs/0805.1598) — the $O(n)$-time, $O(1)$-space perfect shuffle via cycle leaders at powers of $3$.
